opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to see it is to compare robotics with what happened in language models. Large language models got so capable because they could train on essentially the whole internet: trillions of tokens of text that humans had already produced, for free, over decades. Nobody had to collect that data specifically for AI. It was just there.

Robotics has nothing like that. There is no internet of robot actions. To train a robot, you need data that pairs what the robot sees and feels with what it actually did with its motors: the joint angles, the forces, the timing. That kind of data barely exists in the world, so we have to create it ourselves, and that is very expensive. Usually it means a person teleoperating a robot, one demonstration at a time, for hours. Even the biggest robot datasets today are tiny compared with what we use for language or vision, maybe several orders of magnitude smaller.

There's also a diversity problem. It isn't enough to have many hours of data. You need many different environments, objects, lighting conditions, and tasks, because the real world is very long-tailed. A robot trained in one lab kitchen often fails in someone else's kitchen. Collecting data that covers that variety in the physical world is slow. You can't just spin up more servers. You need more robots, more people, and more physical spaces.

And the hardware isn't standardized. Data collected on one robot arm doesn't transfer cleanly to a different arm or a humanoid with different kinematics. So the data we do have is fragmented across embodiments.

That's why I see data as the fundamental bottleneck. The algorithms have improved a lot, and we've shown that the same recipes that work for foundation models, such as large transformers and pretraining followed by fine-tuning, also work for robots. But scaling laws only help if you can scale the data. That's why much of the field's energy is going into ways around the problem: simulation and sim-to-real transfer, learning from human videos, cross-embodiment datasets, and using vision-language models to bring in internet knowledge. Whoever solves the data problem, or finds a scalable way to generate useful robot experience, will likely unlock the next big leap in robotics.

r001.rationale: It contrasts language models’ access to trillions of freely available internet tokens with robotics’ lack of an existing supply of robot action data, which must be collected.

r002.rationale: It explains that the long-tailed physical world requires data across many environments, objects, lighting conditions, and tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is this: if you look at why large language models and vision models suddenly worked, the architecture was important, but the real fuel was the internet. Decades of humans writing text and uploading images gave those models trillions of tokens to learn from, essentially for free. Robotics has nothing like that. There is no internet of robot actions. Nobody has been quietly recording, for thirty years, what torque a motor should apply when you pick up a wet cup from a sink.

So when we try to apply the same recipe, pretraining a big model on a lot of diverse data and then fine-tuning, we hit a wall almost immediately. The data has to be collected physically. You need real robots, in real environments, with real people teleoperating them or demonstrating tasks. That is slow, expensive, and it breaks. A good teleoperation setup might give you a few hundred successful demonstrations a day. Compare that to how many sentences exist on the web, and you see the gap is not two times or ten times, it is many orders of magnitude.

The second issue is that the data we do collect is narrow. A lab will gather a lot of episodes of one robot, in one room, doing a handful of tasks. The model learns that room very well, and then you move the table ten centimeters or change the lighting, and performance drops. Diversity matters as much as volume, and diversity in the physical world is extremely costly to produce because every new scene, object, and embodiment has to be set up by hand.

The third issue is that robot data is not just observations, it is actions, and actions have no natural ground truth. With text, the next word is the label. With robots, the "right" action depends on the embodiment, the controller, the sensor latency. Data collected on one arm often does not transfer cleanly to another. So even when groups try to pool their datasets, which I think is a very good thing, you still face the question of how to make this heterogeneous data actually useful to one model.

That is why I spend a lot of my time thinking about simulation. Simulation is the closest thing we have to an internet for robots, because you can generate essentially unlimited, diverse, perfectly labeled experience. The challenge, of course, is the sim-to-real gap, and that gap is also fundamentally a data problem: how do you make synthetic data close enough to reality that the policy still works when it leaves the computer. We have made a lot of progress on that for locomotion, where the physics is relatively well understood, and I think the frontier now is extending it to manipulation, where contact, deformable objects, and visual realism are much harder.

So when I say data is the bottleneck, I do not mean the algorithms are solved. I mean that if someone handed us a thousand times more diverse, high-quality robot data tomorrow, I believe our current methods would already produce dramatically more capable robots. We are not in that situation for data, and until we find a scalable source, whether that is simulation, human video, or very large fleets of robots learning together, progress will be gated by how much experience we can afford to collect.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the vast, freely available web data used to train language and vision models with robotics’ lack of an existing supply of robot-action data, which must be collected physically.

r002.rationale: It explains that robot data is often narrow and that changing a scene, object, or embodiment can hurt performance, so robots need diverse data across physical environments.

astra-6.text:
I think data is a fundamental bottleneck because robots have to learn how to interact with the physical world, and collecting examples of those interactions is difficult. For language models, there’s an enormous amount of text already available on the internet. In robotics, we need data that connects what a robot sees, the action it takes, and what happens afterward. You can watch a video of someone opening a door, but that video doesn’t directly tell a robot how much force to apply or how to adjust its grip when it starts to slip.

Collecting that experience on real robots takes time and hardware, and it involves wear, failures, and safety considerations. And the diversity matters as much as the quantity. A robot might learn to pick up an object in one lab, but struggle when the lighting changes, the object is unfamiliar, or the surface is slippery.

Simulation can help us generate experience at scale, but it doesn’t perfectly reproduce the real world, especially contact and friction. So the challenge is getting enough diverse, useful experience—and making sure that what the robot learns transfers to the environments where we actually want it to work.

r001.rationale: Contrasts the enormous amount of internet text available for language models with the difficulty of collecting the interaction data robots need.

r002.rationale: Explains that robots encounter varied real-world conditions, such as changing lighting, unfamiliar objects, and slippery surfaces, so training experience must be diverse.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental challenge is that robots need to learn from interacting with the physical world, and collecting those interactions is expensive and slow. You need hardware, you need to maintain it, and when the robot makes a mistake, it can fall or damage something. So you can’t scale data collection as easily as you can in the digital world.

And robotics needs a tremendous amount of diversity. If a robot learns to pick up a cup in one room, that doesn’t necessarily mean it can pick up a different cup under different lighting, or with clutter around it. Getting a demonstration to work is very different from getting a system to work reliably across all those conditions.

That’s why I see data as such a fundamental bottleneck. We have powerful learning methods, but we need enough diverse, useful experience to train them. Simulation can help us scale that experience, but then we have to make sure what the robot learns transfers to the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics data collection is expensive and harder to scale than data collection in the digital world, but it does not state that language-model training data is readily available or that robotics lacks an existing data supply.

r002.rationale: The response links robotics’ need for diverse data to varying physical conditions, including different rooms, lighting, cups, and clutter.
